opus-5.5.text:
I think they're related, but they're not the same thing, and it's worth pulling them apart.

Current language models are pretty good at what you might call fast pattern completion. They've absorbed an enormous amount from training. But they lack a couple of things humans have. One is episodic memory: a person can experience something once, store it, and come back to it later. A language model has its weights, which change slowly through training, and its context window, which is a kind of working memory. Nothing really sits in between. There's no mechanism for learning something specific quickly and retaining it in a structured way. That's part of why these models need so much data. Humans learn a lot from very few examples because we can grab a specific experience and hold onto it.

System 2 thinking is something else. It's deliberate reasoning: searching through possibilities, checking whether what you're saying actually makes sense, considering alternatives before committing. Language models have been weak there too, though people are making progress with chain-of-thought, search, and so on.

The connection is that deliberate reasoning often depends on retrieving specific things. When I work through a hard problem, I'm pulling up particular cases I've seen and testing ideas against them. If you can't store and recall episodes, your reasoning is limited to whatever's compressed in the weights or happens to be in the context. And in the other direction, good System 2 processes help decide what's worth remembering and how to use it.

So I don't think these are fundamental blockers. They're architectural gaps people know about and are working on. I expect fairly clean solutions to both over the next few years, and when they arrive, a lot of the remaining distance to more general capabilities closes quickly.

r001.rationale: The response says episodic memory and System 2 are related but not the same, and describes them as distinct capabilities.

r002.rationale: It explains that reasoning through hard problems involves recalling specific past cases and testing ideas against them, linking episodic memory to ways of thinking through problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think they're actually quite closely related, and the way I'd frame it is that current models are missing both, and they're missing them for somewhat similar reasons.

So let's start with episodic memory. If you look at the human brain, we have this ability to very rapidly learn specific things. You have a conversation with someone, something happens, and you remember that specific episode. The hippocampus is doing a lot of this, and it's a kind of fast learning system. It's not the slow, gradual, statistical learning that the cortex is doing over years of experience. And current language models basically only have the slow kind. They learn everything in pretraining, the weights get fixed, and then at deployment they've got a context window. The context window is a sort of poor man's episodic memory. It's working memory, really. Once something falls out of context, it's gone, and the model never consolidates it into anything lasting. So you've got this very long, slow learning phase, and a very short, volatile scratchpad, and nothing in between. Humans have that in-between layer, and I think that's a real gap.

Now, System 2 thinking, in the Kahneman sense, is deliberate, sequential, effortful reasoning. You're not just pattern-matching an answer, you're searching, you're checking, you're considering alternatives, you're noticing when you've made a mistake and backtracking. And what the field has found is that you can get a surprising amount of this out of a language model just by letting it generate a lot of intermediate tokens before it commits to an answer. Chain of thought, and then the more recent models that are trained to reason at length with reinforcement learning. That's a sort of System 2 emerging on top of a System 1 substrate, which is honestly roughly how I'd describe what happens in people too. Our deliberate reasoning is built out of lots of fast intuitive steps strung together.

Here's where I see the connection. Real System 2 thinking isn't just long reasoning within a single problem. It's reasoning that draws on your own experience. When you deliberate about something, you're pulling in specific past episodes. "Last time I tried this approach it went badly, and here's why." You're retrieving particular memories, not just general knowledge, and you're using them to guide the search. Without episodic memory, a model's System 2 is confined to whatever is in the prompt plus what got baked into the weights. It can't accumulate. It solves a hard problem on Monday, and on Tuesday it has no memory of how it did it, or that it did it at all. So it can't get better at the kind of deliberate reasoning that depends on building up a personal history of what works.

And it goes the other direction too. Episodic memory on its own isn't that useful unless you have the deliberate machinery to decide what's worth storing, to retrieve the right thing at the right time, and to integrate it with the problem in front of you. That's a System 2 job. So I think of them as two halves of one capability, which is the ability to learn continually from experience and to reason over that experience.

People sometimes say, well, retrieval augmented generation solves memory. I don't really buy that. Pulling text out of a database and stuffing it into the context is useful, but it's not the same as a system that has actually learned from an episode and changed how it thinks as a result. The retrieval is dumb, the integration is shallow, and nothing in the underlying model has been updated.

So when I think about what's missing on the path to AGI, this is one of the things I'd point to. Not more pretraining data, not more parameters as such. It's this fast, ongoing learning from experience, and the deliberate reasoning that both feeds it and feeds on it. The current systems are very impressive in a kind of frozen way. They know an enormous amount and they can think fairly carefully about it. But they don't live through anything, if that makes sense, and I think that turns out to matter a lot for the kind of general intelligence we're actually aiming at.

r001.rationale: The response calls episodic memory and System 2 thinking closely related and describes them as two halves of one capability, rather than largely separate.

r002.rationale: It says episodic memories of past approaches guide deliberate search and help a model learn what works when solving problems.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary, but they’re distinct capabilities. Episodic memory is about retaining particular experiences: what you tried, what happened, and the context in which it happened. System 2 thinking is about spending computation on a problem—exploring possibilities, checking an argument, revising a plan—rather than immediately producing an answer.

You can have one without much of the other. A system could remember a great deal but do very little reasoning with it. Or it could reason quite deeply about a problem and then lose everything it discovered when the conversation ends.

The interesting thing is what happens when you bring them together. Suppose a model spends a substantial amount of time solving a difficult problem. You’d like it to retain something useful from that process, so that when it encounters a related problem, it can retrieve the relevant experience and build on it. Otherwise, it’s repeatedly paying the cost of discovering the same thing.

But storing the entire reasoning trace isn’t necessarily the answer. The system has to work out what’s worth remembering, when a memory applies, and whether the conclusion it previously reached was actually correct. Those are themselves reasoning problems. So memory can make deliberation more effective, and deliberation can help determine what gets remembered.

r001.rationale: It calls episodic memory and System 2 thinking distinct capabilities and says a system can have one without much of the other.

r002.rationale: It says memory can preserve useful experience from solving a problem and help with related problems, but does not clearly identify it as a way to learn how to think through problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary, but I wouldn’t identify one with the other. Episodic memory is about retaining particular experiences: what happened, what you tried, and what the outcome was. System 2 thinking is about doing computation at the time you’re trying to solve a problem—considering possibilities, checking your reasoning, perhaps backing up and trying another approach.

You can do that computation without much episodic memory. You could give a model a novel mathematical problem and let it spend a long time working through it. But if it worked on a similar problem yesterday, you’d like it to remember which approaches failed, rather than having to rediscover that every time.

And the relationship goes in the other direction as well. Having a large store of experiences isn’t enough. You need to work out which memories are relevant, whether the circumstances are sufficiently similar, and how to adapt what you learned. That can itself require deliberation.

So I’d expect a capable system to have a loop between the two: retrieve relevant experience, reason about the current situation, take some action, and retain what happened. The interesting question is how to make that loop reliable—especially how the system decides what’s worth remembering and when a remembered experience should influence its reasoning.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the two as complementary concepts: System 2 is computation during problem solving, while episodic memory retains experiences, and each can exist without the other.

r002.rationale: It says episodic memory can preserve which approaches failed on similar problems, so a model can use prior experience instead of rediscovering those approaches.
